title: Shell
subtitle: CLI between you and the kernel — flip for meaning, example, and notes

cards.meaning: Program that provides an interface between the user and the OS kernel
cards.notes: You type commands; the shell interprets them and asks the kernel to do the real work. You almost never talk to the kernel directly.

cards.meaning: Layered path from you (or a script) down to physical devices
cards.notes: Shell = command interpreter. Kernel manages CPU, memory, processes, devices, file systems.

cards.meaning: Manages CPU, memory, processes, devices, and file systems
cards.example: Shell asks the kernel to open files, start processes, talk to hardware
cards.notes: Hardware layer is disks, NIC, RAM, and so on.

cards.meaning: The Bourne Shell — original Unix shell (1970s)
cards.notes: Many scripts still start with #!/bin/sh. Ancestor of bash.

cards.meaning: The C Shell — syntax looks more like the C language
cards.notes: Less common on servers today. Only csh uses % for a normal-user prompt.

cards.meaning: The Korn Shell — Bourne-compatible with extra features
cards.notes: Still seen on some Unix systems.

cards.meaning: GNU Bourne-Again Shell — default interactive shell on most Linux distros
cards.notes: Bourne-compatible plus history, completion, and better scripting. bash = Bourne-Again SHell.

cards.meaning: Usual paths for the Bourne Shell (sh)
cards.notes: On most modern Linux systems /bin/sh is a symlink to bash or dash, but still runs in a more POSIX / Bourne-compatible mode.

cards.meaning: Usual path for the C Shell
cards.notes: Non-root default prompt is %; root is #.

cards.meaning: Usual path for the Korn Shell
cards.notes: Non-root default prompt is $; root is #.
Default interactive shell path on most Linux distros.

cards.meaning: Default non-root prompt for sh, ksh, and bash
cards.notes: $ or % → regular user. Bash includes its version in the default prompt.

cards.meaning: Default non-root prompt for csh only
cards.notes: Only csh uses % for a normal user among the shells in this topic.

cards.meaning: Default root (superuser) prompt across these shells
cards.notes: Hash = extra power. Commands as root can change the whole system.

cards.meaning: Stores your login shell (last field on your user line)
cards.notes: Not always the same as the shell of your current process ($0).

cards.meaning: Shows the login shell from your account (passwd / SHELL var)
cards.notes: Login shell from the account — may differ from the shell you are running right now.

cards.meaning: Name of the current shell process
cards.notes: A leading - often means a login shell.

cards.front: Where shells show up in DevOps
cards.meaning: SSH sessions, CI jobs, Docker ENTRYPOINTs, Ansible, and cloud-init all run shell
cards.example: ssh into a Linux server → you get a shell
cards.notes: Knowing which shell and how it talks to the kernel is the base of this folder.
